steps: Prepare the banana blossom by removing the tough outer purple bracts until you reach the pale heart; slice into thick wedges and soak in acidulated water to prevent browning.
Drain and rinse the young jackfruit, removing any hard core pieces, and pat dry.
In a large bowl, whisk together coconut milk, ginger-garlic paste, turmeric, chili powder, garam masala, and salt.
Toss the jackfruit pieces and banana blossom wedges in the marinade and let sit for at least 30 minutes.
Thread the marinated jackfruit and banana blossom alternately onto soaked wooden skewers.
Heat coconut oil in a grill pan over medium-high heat and sear the skewers for 4-5 minutes per side until charred and tender.
Garnish with flash-fried curry leaves and a squeeze of fresh lemon juice before serving.
Scrub the black clams thoroughly under cold water to remove any mud or grit.
Carefully pry open each clam over a bowl to catch all the dark, briny liquor; extract the meat and place it into the bowl with the juice.
Season the meat and juice with salt, pepper, garlic paste, and rocoto paste, stirring gently.
Add the finely diced red onion and minced ají limo, then pour over the fresh lime juice.
Toss in the fresh cilantro and mix well; let it marinate for no more than 2-5 minutes to keep the clams tender.
Serve immediately in small bowls, accompanied by slices of sweet potato and choclo.
Mix flour, yeast, sugar, and salt; gradually add warm water, milk, and a splash of oil to form a smooth dough. Let rise for 1.5 hours.
Grate the Sulguni and Imeruli cheeses together, mixing in one egg to bind the filling into a thick paste.
Divide the dough into balls; roll each into an oval and roll up the long sides toward the center, pinching the ends to form a boat shape.
Fill the center of the boat generously with the cheese mixture and brush the dough edges with egg wash.
Bake at 230°C (450°F) for 12-15 minutes until the crust is golden and cheese is bubbling.
Remove from oven, use a spoon to make a well in the cheese, and drop a raw egg yolk into the center.
Add a thick slice of butter and return to the oven for 1 minute (the yolk should remain runny). Serve hot to be mixed at the table.
Blend shallots, garlic, ginger, and chilies into a smooth spice paste (bumbu).
In a heavy-bottomed pot, combine coconut milk, spice paste, lemongrass, galangal, and turmeric leaf over medium heat.
Bring to a boil, then add the beef and lower heat to a simmer, stirring occasionally.
Once the coconut milk thickens and turns oily (kalio stage), add the toasted coconut (kerisik) and salt.
Continue cooking on very low heat, stirring constantly, until the liquid evaporates and the spices dark brown and cling to the meat.
Serve at room temperature; it’s best eaten the following day.
Remove seeds from chiles and fry the seeds in a pan until completely charred and black; soak the seeds in water to remove bitterness.
Toast the chiles lightly, then soak in hot water until soft; blend with the charred seeds.
Sauté onions, garlic, raisins, almonds, and plantains in lard until golden; blend with spices and bread to create a thick paste.
Fry the combined pastes in a large pot with lard until fragrant and darkened.
Slowly whisk in chicken stock and the chocolate, simmering until the sauce reaches a velvet-thick consistency.
Serve over poached turkey or chicken with a garnish of sesame seeds.
Grind shallots, garlic, ginger, turmeric, and chilies into a paste; crush the andaliman pepper separately.
Sauté the spice paste with lemongrass and lime leaves until aromatic.
Add the pork cubes and cook until the meat is browned and juices are released.
Add a small amount of water and simmer until the pork is tender and the liquid has reduced by half.
Lower the heat and slowly pour in the blood, stirring constantly to prevent curdling until the sauce turns dark and thickens.
Finish with crushed andaliman pepper for the signature numbing citrus finish.
Blanch grape leaves in boiling water for 2 minutes if fresh, or rinse thoroughly if brined.
In a bowl, combine ground beef, rice, onions, chopped herbs, tomato paste, salt, and pepper; mix by hand until tacky.
Place a leaf flat, add a tablespoon of filling at the base, and roll tightly into a small cylinder, tucking the sides in.
Line the bottom of a heavy pot with torn leaves and pack the tolma in tight, circular layers.
Add enough water or light broth to barely cover them; weight them down with an inverted plate to prevent unrolling.
Simmer on low heat for 45-50 minutes until the rice is tender and water is absorbed.
Serve hot with a side of matzoon mixed with minced garlic.
Simmer beef shank with star anise, cassia, ginger, and peppercorns for 3 hours; strain to keep the broth crystal clear.
Mix flour with water and alkaline solution (peng hui); knead until the gluten is highly elastic and the dough doesn't snap when stretched.
Pull and fold the dough repeatedly into thin strands (or slice into thin ribbons if hand-pulling is too technical).
Boil the fresh noodles for only 1-2 minutes until they float.
Parboil the radish slices in the beef broth until translucent.
Assemble by placing noodles in a bowl, topping with thin slices of the cooked beef and radish.
Ladle the hot, clear broth over the top and garnish heavily with cilantro, scallions, and a signature swirl of deep red chili oil.
Make a 'rof' (herb paste) by pounding parsley, garlic, and chili; poke holes in the fish and stuff it with this paste.
Sear the fish in oil until golden, then remove and set aside.
Fry onions and tomato paste in the same oil until the oil separates; add the fermented fish (guédj) for deep umami.
Add water, cassava, eggplant, and carrots; simmer until vegetables are tender, then remove them and set aside.
Wash the broken rice and steam it over the bubbling broth for 15 minutes.
Add the pre-steamed rice into the broth, ensuring the liquid level is just right to absorb without burning.
Arrange the fish and vegetables back on top of the rice for the final 10 minutes of steaming. Serve on a large communal platter.
Boil the lamb chunks with cardamom and bay leaves, skimming the foam until the meat is halfway cooked; drain and set the meat aside.
Slowly whisk the liquefied jameed into a large pot and bring to a gentle simmer, stirring constantly in one direction to prevent curdling.
Add the lamb to the jameed sauce and simmer on low for 1-2 hours until the meat is 'falling off the bone' tender.
Cook the rice with ghee and turmeric to give it a vibrant yellow color and rich aroma.
To assemble, layer a large platter with shrak bread and ladle a small amount of jameed sauce to soak it.
Mound the rice over the bread, arrange the lamb pieces on top, and pour more sauce over the entire dish.
Garnish heavily with toasted nuts and parsley. Serve the remaining sauce in a bowl on the side to be poured by guests.
Pat the cuy completely dry; this is the most important step for achieving crispy skin.
Create a marinade by mixing huacatay, garlic, cumin, ají amarillo, and chicha de jora.
Rub the marinade inside the cavity and all over the skin; let it rest in the fridge for at least 4 hours (uncovered to dry the skin).
Traditionally roasted on a spit, but for home use: place on a wire rack over a baking tray.
Roast at 180°C (350°F) for 45 minutes, then increase to 220°C (425°F) for 10 minutes to blister the skin.
Serve whole or halved, accompanied by 'papa helada' (boiled potatoes) and an onion salsa (sarsa criolla).
Thaw the pure açaí pulp slightly until it reaches a thick, creamy, pudding-like consistency.
Pour the deep purple cream into a clay bowl; do not blend with bananas or juice.
Prepare the fried fish separately, seasoned simply with salt and lime.
Serve the bowl of açaí alongside the hot fish.
The diner sprinkles the crunchy manioc flour over the açaí with each spoonful, alternating bites with the salty fish.
If desired, a very small amount of sugar can be sprinkled on top to balance the earthy bitterness.

ingredients.name: carrots (mix of yellow and orange, julienned)

steps: Heat the fat in a heavy cast-iron Kazan until smoking; sear the meat until deeply browned and remove.
Fry the onions until golden brown, then add the carrots and cook until softened; return the meat to the pot.
Add water to barely cover, add spices, barberries, and chickpeas; simmer for 40 minutes to create the 'Zirvak' (flavor base).
Place whole garlic bulbs into the liquid, then layer the washed rice evenly over the top—do not stir.
Add boiling water over a slotted spoon so as not to disturb the rice layer, until it's 2cm above the rice.
Cook on high until water evaporates, then poke holes to the bottom for steam, cover tightly, and steam on very low for 20 minutes.
Remove garlic, mix the layers thoroughly, and serve on a large 'Lagan' platter.
Whisk rice flour, turmeric, coconut milk, and sparkling water (for extra bubbles) into a thin batter; let rest for 30 minutes.
Heat a large wok or skillet with oil; sauté a few slices of pork and shrimp until just cooked.
Pour a thin layer of batter into the pan, swirling quickly to coat the edges; it should make a loud 'hissing' sound.
Place a handful of bean sprouts on one half, cover with a lid for 2 minutes to steam the sprouts.
Remove lid and cook for another 2 minutes until the edges are crispy and start to lift away from the pan.
Fold the crepe in half and slide onto a plate.
To eat: tear a piece of the crepe, wrap it inside a large mustard or lettuce leaf with fresh herbs, and dip in nuoc cham.
Slow-cook the minced onions in a dry pot over low heat for 45 minutes, stirring constantly until they lose all moisture and turn into a jam-like paste.
Add the niter kibbeh and let it melt into the onions; then stir in the berbere spice and cook for another 15 minutes.
Add the garlic-ginger paste and a splash of wine or broth if the mixture is too dry; the base should be deep mahogany.
Add the chicken drumsticks, coating them thoroughly in the onion paste; cover and simmer for 45 minutes until tender.
Make small incisions in the hard-boiled eggs and add them to the pot for the last 10 minutes to soak up the sauce.
Finish with a squeeze of lemon juice.
Serve on a large piece of injera; use the bread as your only utensil to scoop up the chicken and sauce.
In a tall glass, layer the bottom with sweetened beans, macapuno, kaong, and other preserved fruits.
Fill the glass with finely shaved ice until it reaches the brim.
Pour the evaporated milk generously over the ice, letting it seep down to the bottom layers.
Top the ice with a scoop of ube halaya and a square of leche flan.
Place a final scoop of ube ice cream on top and sprinkle with crunchy pinipig.
Serve with a long spoon; the diner must vigorously mix everything together before eating.
Thread the lamb sweetbreads onto a horizontal skewer.
Carefully wrap the cleaned intestines around the sweetbreads tightly to form a thick log (spit).
Roast over a charcoal fire (or a high-heat grill), rotating constantly until the exterior is deeply browned and crispy.
Slice a portion of the meat off the log and place it on a flat griddle.
Chop the meat finely with spatulas on the heat, mixing in the diced tomatoes and peppers.
Season aggressively with oregano, pul biber, cumin, and salt.
Slice the bread open, press it onto the meat to soak up the fats, then fill with the chopped mixture. Serve hot.
Mash the boiled potatoes while hot and mix with the twaróg until smooth; season heavily with black pepper.
Sauté half the onions in butter until golden brown and stir them into the potato-cheese filling.
Knead flour and warm water into a soft, elastic dough; let it rest under a warm bowl for 30 minutes.
Roll dough thin and cut circles using a glass; place a spoonful of filling in the center and pinch edges to seal.
Boil in salted water until they float, then cook for 2 more minutes.
Sauté the remaining onions in plenty of butter until caramelized; toss the boiled pierogi in the onion butter to brown slightly.
Serve with a side of cold sour cream.
Heat oil and sauté star anise, cinnamon stick, and curry leaves; add onions and ginger-garlic paste until golden.
Add the Durban curry powder and tomatoes, cooking until the oil begins to separate from the spice base.
Add the meat and brown thoroughly; then add potatoes and enough water to create a thick, rich gravy.
Simmer for 1 hour until the meat is tender and the potatoes have slightly thickened the sauce.
Cut the loaf of bread in half (or quarters) and hollow out the center, keeping the bread 'plug' intact.
Ladle the hot curry into the bread cavity, letting the gravy soak into the walls of the loaf.
Place the 'plug' back on top and serve with a side of carrot salad (sambal).
Fry the curry paste in a thick layer of coconut cream until the oil splits and becomes fragrant.
Add chicken thighs and remaining coconut milk; simmer gently for 45 minutes until the meat is tender.
Season the broth with palm sugar and fish sauce to balance the spicy, salty, and sweet notes.
Boil 3/4 of the egg noodles until soft and set aside.
Deep-fry the remaining 1/4 of the noodles until they are golden and extremely crispy.
Place the soft noodles in a bowl, ladle over the chicken and plenty of broth.
Top with the crispy noodles and serve with a side plate of pickled mustard greens, raw shallots, and lime.
Marinate the eel slices in white wine, salt, and pepper for at least 30 minutes.
In a large pot, sauté the onions, garlic, carrots, and tomatoes until soft.
Add the paprika and oregano, then pour in the fish stock and the marinade from the eel.
Add the potatoes and simmer for 15 minutes until they begin to soften.
Gently place the eel slices into the pot. Simmer for another 10-12 minutes until the fish is opaque and firm.
Just before serving, stir in the heavy cream and remove from heat.
Serve in heated clay bowls, garnished with fresh cilantro.

ingredients.name: Goat meat (with bone, cut into pieces)

steps: Marinate the goat meat in cumin, garlic, salt, and half of the Chicha de Jora for at least 2 hours.
In a large heavy-bottomed pot, heat the achiote oil and brown the goat meat in batches. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, sauté the onions, bell pepper, and tomatoes until soft and fragrant.
Return the meat to the pot and add the remaining Chicha de Jora, Naranjilla juice, and panela.
Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to a low simmer. Cover and cook for 2 to 2.5 hours until the meat is falling off the bone.
Uncover for the last 20 minutes to allow the sauce to reduce into a thick, glossy consistency.
Stir in the fresh cilantro just before serving with yellow rice and maduros (fried ripe plantains).
Soak the salt beef in cold water overnight in the refrigerator to remove excess salt. Rinse before cooking.
Place the yellow split peas into a cotton 'pudding bag' or several layers of cheesecloth, tying it securely but leaving room for the peas to expand.
Place the salt beef and the pea bag into a large stockpot. Cover with fresh water and bring to a boil.
Reduce heat and simmer for about 1.5 to 2 hours until the beef begins to soften.
Add the turnip, carrots, and cabbage wedges to the pot. Simmer for 20 minutes.
Add the potatoes and continue simmering for another 20-25 minutes until all vegetables are fork-tender.
Remove the pea bag. Empty the peas into a bowl, add butter and black pepper, and mash until smooth to create the pease pudding.
Serve the meat and vegetables on a large platter with the pease pudding on the side.

ingredients.name: Reindeer fat or beef tallow (finely shredded)

steps: Place the shredded fat in a large bowl and cream it by hand (the heat from your hand is traditional for achieving the right texture) until it becomes light and fluffy.
Slowly add the seal oil or vegetable oil, a little at a time, while continuing to whip the mixture vigorously.
Add a small amount of water or snow to the mixture to increase the volume and achieve a white, creamy consistency.
If using sugar, fold it in slowly until dissolved.
Gently fold in the wild berries by hand so they remain whole and do not bleed too much color into the white base.
Chill the mixture in a cold area or freezer until firm but scoopable.
Serve immediately as a high-energy treat or side dish.

ingredients.name: Lamb leg or shoulder (cubed into 1-inch pieces)

steps: Cut the lamb into uniform 1-inch cubes, trimming excess fat but leaving some for flavor.
Season the cubes generously with garlic salt and black pepper, tossing to coat evenly.
Heat oil in a deep fryer or heavy pot to 190°C (375°F).
Fry the cubes in small batches for 3-4 minutes until the exterior is deeply golden and crispy but the interior remains pink and juicy.
Drain on paper towels and hit immediately with another dusting of garlic salt while still glistening.
Spear each cube with a toothpick and pile onto a plate alongside saltine crackers.
Dissolve yeast and sugar in warm water. Let it bloom for 5 minutes until frothy.
Mix flour and salt, then add the yeast mixture and olive oil. Knead for 8 to 10 minutes until the dough is smooth and elastic.
Cover and let rise in a warm spot for 1 hour until doubled in size.
Punch down the dough and divide into 8 equal portions. Roll each into a flat oval.
Place a pepperoni stick (or a row of overlapping slices) along the center of each oval. Fold the dough over and pinch the seam and ends shut tightly.
Place seam-side down on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Let rise for 20 minutes.
Bake at 190°C (375°F) for 18 to 20 minutes until golden brown. The rendered pepperoni fat will have soaked into the bread from the inside.
Cool on a wire rack. Serve at room temperature, exactly as the miners did.
Whisk together buckwheat flour, all-purpose flour, baking powder, and salt in a large bowl.
Add the cold water and stir until combined, then pour in the boiling water while stirring constantly. The batter should be thin and pourable, like crepe batter.
Let the batter rest for 5 minutes. It will thicken slightly.
Heat a lightly greased griddle or cast-iron skillet over medium heat.

Pour about 1/3 cup of batter onto the griddle and spread into a thin circle. Do NOT flip. Cook on one side only until the entire surface is covered with tiny holes and the top looks dry (about 2 minutes).
Slide the ploye off the griddle and stack on a plate. Repeat with the remaining batter.
Serve warm, spread with butter and rolled up, or use as a wrap for cretons, baked beans, or stew.
Fry or bake the french fries until golden and crispy. Keep warm.
Cook the hamburger patties (or warm the ham slices) to your liking. Set aside.
For the Welsh rarebit sauce: melt butter in a saucepan over medium-low heat. Add milk, beer, mustard powder, Worcestershire, and cayenne. Heat until steaming but not boiling.
Gradually stir in the shredded cheddar, a handful at a time, stirring constantly until you have a smooth, thick cheese sauce. Do not let it boil or it will break.
Toast the bread and place two slices on each plate.
Top each slice with a hamburger patty, then pile the hot french fries over everything.
Pour the cheese sauce generously over the entire construction. Serve immediately with a knife and fork.
Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Prepare a large bowl of ice water.
Separate the geoduck's siphon from the body by cutting around the base of the shell. Remove the gut ball and set aside (can be used for chowder).
Dunk the siphon into boiling water for exactly 10 seconds, then immediately plunge it into the ice water. The outer skin will loosen.
Peel away the tough outer skin of the siphon to reveal the smooth, pale flesh underneath.
Split the siphon lengthwise and rinse under cold water to remove any sand.
Slice the siphon crosswise into paper-thin pieces, angling the knife at about 45 degrees for maximum surface area.
Arrange the slices on a chilled plate over shredded daikon and shiso leaves. Serve immediately with soy sauce, fresh wasabi, and lemon wedges.
Whisk together flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt. Add milk, melted butter, and vanilla, stirring until just combined. Do not overmix.
Pour the batter into a buttered 9x13 inch baking dish and spread evenly.
In a saucepan, combine the maple syrup, heavy cream, and butter. Heat over medium until the butter melts and the mixture is hot and smooth. Do not boil.
Gently pour the hot maple cream sauce over the raw batter. It will look wrong. Trust the process.
Bake at 175°C (350°F) for 35 to 40 minutes until the cake layer is golden and a toothpick comes out clean. The syrup will have sunk to the bottom and turned into a thick, caramelized sauce.
Let cool for 10 minutes (the sauce is volcanic), then scoop into bowls, making sure to spoon up the maple sauce from the bottom with each serving.
Dissolve the achiote paste in bitter orange juice, then blend with garlic, peppercorns, oregano, and salt into a smooth marinade.
Score the pork deeply and rub the marinade into every cut and surface. Refrigerate overnight or at least 4 hours.
Pass the banana leaves briefly over an open flame or hot pan to make them pliable.
Line a deep roasting pan with overlapping banana leaves, leaving enough overhang to wrap the top. Place the marinated pork inside and pour over any remaining marinade.
Fold the banana leaves tightly over the pork, then seal the pan with a double layer of aluminum foil.
Roast at 150°C (300°F) for 4 to 5 hours until the pork shreds effortlessly with a fork.
While the pork roasts, thinly slice the red onions and quick-pickle them in bitter orange juice with a whole habanero and a pinch of salt for at least 1 hour.
Shred the pork in its juices and serve on warm corn tortillas, topped with the pickled onions and a spoonful of the pan juices.
Place the chicken, beef chuck, and oxtails in a very large stockpot. Cover with cold water and bring to a boil, skimming the foam as it rises.
Reduce heat and simmer for 2 to 3 hours until all meats are falling apart tender.
Remove the meats, shred or chop them, and return to the pot. Discard bones and excess fat.
Add onions, celery, carrots, and crushed tomatoes. Simmer for another hour, stirring occasionally.
Add potatoes, cabbage, corn, and bay leaves. Continue simmering for 45 minutes until the vegetables are soft and the stew is thick enough that a wooden spoon stands up in it.
Season generously with salt and pepper. Remove bay leaves.
Serve in deep bowls with crusty bread. Tastes even better reheated the next day.
Toss the sliced peaches with half the sugar, cinnamon, and nutmeg. Let them macerate for 20 minutes until juicy.
Whisk together flour, remaining sugar, baking powder, milk, melted butter, and vanilla into a thin, pourable batter.
Pour the fruit and all its juices into a large, deep baking dish (at least 9x13 inches).
Pour the batter evenly over the top of the fruit. Do not stir.
Bake at 175°C (350°F) for 45 to 50 minutes until the crust is golden brown and the fruit is bubbling through.
While the sonker bakes, make the 'dip': heat milk, sugar, butter, and vanilla in a small saucepan until warm and smooth.
Serve generous scoops of the hot sonker in bowls, ladled with the warm milk dip.

ingredients.name: Shortening or marrow fat (for greasing stone)

steps: Sift the blue cornmeal into a large traditional clay or mixing bowl.
Dissolve the juniper ash in cold water and strain through a fine cloth into the cornmeal to remove any grit.
Gradually add the boiling water to the cornmeal mixture, stirring constantly until it forms a smooth, thin, pourable batter with no lumps.
Heat the Piki stone (sandstone slab) over a steady fire until a drop of water sizzles and dances on the surface (approx. 350°F).
Lightly grease the stone with a small amount of fat or oil using a clean cloth.
Using your fingers or a flat scoop, quickly smear a very thin layer of batter across the hot stone in a single, fluid motion.
Wait seconds for the edges to curl and the bread to turn translucent. Gently peel the sheet away from the stone.
While still hot and pliable, place the sheet on a flat surface and roll it tightly into a scroll. Repeat the process, often layering two sheets together before rolling.
Let the rolls cool until crisp and brittle.
Prepare the sattu filling by mixing sattu with chopped green chilies, ajwain, kalonji, 2 tablespoons mustard oil, lemon juice, and salt. Add just enough water to make a moist but not wet mixture.
Make a firm dough from whole wheat flour, a pinch of salt, and water. Let it rest covered for 20 minutes.
Divide the dough into golf ball sized portions. Flatten each ball, place a generous spoonful of sattu filling in the center, and seal the edges, rolling gently back into a smooth ball.
Roast the stuffed balls directly over a charcoal or wood fire (or on a gas flame using a wire rack), turning frequently until the exterior is evenly charred and crispy all around, about 15 minutes.
For the chokha, roast the whole eggplant and tomatoes directly over flame until the skin is completely blackened and the flesh is soft and smoky.
Peel the charred eggplant and tomatoes, then mash them together with the boiled potatoes, minced garlic, remaining mustard oil, salt, and chopped coriander into a coarse, rustic mash.
Crack each litti open with your thumb, drench generously with melted ghee, and serve hot alongside the chokha.
Slice the lamb into thin, flat pieces about 5mm thick, trimming off any excess fat or sinew.
Make the marinade by combining raw papaya paste, ginger paste, garlic paste, lime juice, red chili powder, turmeric, coriander powder, black pepper, and salt in a large bowl.
Coat the lamb slices thoroughly in the marinade, tuck in the slit green chilies, cover, and refrigerate for at least 2 hours (overnight is ideal for maximum tenderness).
Heat a thick granite slab, cast iron griddle, or heavy stone plate over high flame for at least 20 minutes until it is searingly hot. Do not oil the surface.
Place the marinated lamb slices directly onto the hot stone in a single layer. They should sizzle immediately on contact.
Cook for 60 to 90 seconds per side, pressing gently with a spatula, until charred on the outside and just cooked through.
Transfer to a warm plate, scatter with fresh mint and coriander leaves, and serve immediately with roomali roti or naan.
Tear or roughly chop the day old roti into small, irregular strips about the size of your thumb.
Heat oil on a large flat griddle or heavy skillet over high heat. Add curry leaves, garlic, and sliced onions, stir frying until the onions soften.
Add the shredded chicken and cook through, then toss in the leeks, cabbage, and carrots, stir frying for 2 minutes until slightly wilted but still crunchy.
Push the vegetables to one side, crack the eggs onto the griddle, and scramble them roughly before mixing everything together.
Add the roti strips to the griddle. Using two heavy metal spatulas or cleavers, chop and toss the roti into the vegetable and egg mixture with a rapid rhythmic motion.
Season with curry powder, chili flakes, soy sauce, and salt. Pour in the curry sauce and continue chopping and tossing until the roti has absorbed the sauce and everything is well combined.
Serve immediately on a plate or in a banana leaf, with a side of curry sauce for extra dipping.
Rinse the smoked pork chunks under water to remove surface soot, then boil them in a pot of water for 15 minutes to soften slightly. Drain and set aside.
If using whole fermented bamboo shoot, slice it into thin strips. Rinse once if the sourness is too intense, but keep some tang.
Heat mustard oil in a heavy pot until it just begins to smoke. Add the crushed ginger, garlic, and chopped onion, stirring until the onion turns translucent.
Add the boiled smoked pork chunks and sear for 5 minutes, letting them pick up some color on the edges.
Stir in the axone paste, breaking it up so it coats the pork evenly. Cook for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the bamboo shoot strips and whole Raja Mircha. Pour in the water, bring to a boil, then reduce to a low simmer.
Cover and cook for 40 to 50 minutes until the pork is completely tender and the broth has reduced to a thick, concentrated sauce. Adjust salt and serve with steamed rice.
Soak the yellow and black mustard seeds in water for at least 30 minutes, then grind them into a smooth, pungent paste using a mortar and pestle or blender with minimal water.
Rub the Hilsa steaks gently with turmeric and a pinch of salt. Set aside for 10 minutes.
Heat mustard oil in a wide, heavy pan until it reaches smoking point, then let it cool slightly. This tames the raw bitterness of the oil.
Lightly fry the Hilsa steaks for about a minute on each side just to seal them. Remove carefully and set aside.
In the same oil, add nigella seeds and let them splutter. Stir in the ground mustard paste, remaining turmeric, and salt. Cook for 2 minutes, adding water to loosen it into a sauce consistency.
Gently place the Hilsa steaks back into the mustard sauce. Tuck in the slit green chilies, drizzle a tablespoon of raw mustard oil over the top, and cover.
Simmer on low heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the fish is cooked through and the sauce has thickened around it. Serve immediately with steamed white rice.

ingredients.name: boneless lamb (preferably leg, all fat removed)

steps: Cut the lamb and lamb fat into small pieces. Using a heavy wooden mallet or meat pounder on a flat stone slab, pound the meat and fat together relentlessly until it becomes a completely smooth, paste like consistency with absolutely no visible fibers. This traditionally takes 1 to 2 hours.

Season the meat paste with half the fennel powder, a pinch of dry ginger, and salt. Mix thoroughly, then shape into large, smooth meatballs roughly the size of a tennis ball. Handle them gently as they are delicate.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a gentle boil. Carefully lower the meatballs in and poach them for 20 to 25 minutes until they float and are cooked through. Remove with a slotted spoon and set aside.
Soak the saffron strands in warm milk and set aside. Whisk the hung yogurt until completely smooth with no lumps.
Heat mustard oil or ghee in a heavy bottomed pot. Add bay leaves, cardamom, cloves, and cinnamon, letting them crackle for 30 seconds.

Lower the heat and slowly add the whisked yogurt, stirring constantly in one direction to prevent splitting. Add the remaining fennel powder, dry ginger, and salt. Let the sauce simmer gently for 15 minutes until it thickens slightly.

Slide the poached meatballs into the yogurt sauce, pour over the saffron milk, and simmer on the lowest heat for another 10 minutes so the meatballs absorb the flavors. Serve warm with steamed Kashmiri rice.
Boil the pork shoulder, liver, and heart together in salted water until just cooked through, about 20 minutes. Reserve the cooking liquid. Cut all the meat into small, uniform cubes.
Soak the Kashmiri chilies in warm vinegar for 15 minutes, then grind them into a smooth paste along with the cumin, peppercorns, cloves, cinnamon, garlic, and ginger.
Heat oil in a heavy pot and fry the chopped onions until deep golden brown.
Add the ground spice paste and turmeric, frying on medium heat for 5 minutes until the oil separates and the raw smell disappears.
Add the cubed pork, liver, and heart. Stir well to coat everything in the spice paste. Pour in about half a cup of the reserved cooking liquid.
Stir in the remaining vinegar, tamarind pulp, jaggery, and salt. Bring to a simmer, then cook uncovered on low heat for 30 minutes until the sauce is dark, thick, and clinging to the meat.
Remove from heat, let it cool completely, and refrigerate. Reheat and serve the next day (or better yet, on day three) with warm pav or sannas.
Soak the dried sangri beans in water overnight or for at least 8 hours. Soak the dried ker berries separately for 2 hours. Drain both and squeeze out excess water.
Heat mustard oil in a heavy pan until it reaches smoking point, then let it cool for 30 seconds to remove the raw bitterness.
Add cumin seeds, mustard seeds, and dried red chilies to the oil. Let them splutter and crackle for a few seconds.
Add asafoetida and turmeric, stir once, then immediately add the drained sangri beans. Cook on medium heat for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the drained ker berries, red chili powder, and coriander powder. Stir well and cook for another 8 to 10 minutes until both the ker and sangri are tender but still hold their shape.
Sprinkle the amchur powder and salt, toss everything together, and cook for a final 2 minutes. The dish should be dry with no liquid remaining.
Serve hot with bajra roti (millet flatbread) or plain chapati.

To prepare khar liquid at home, dry the peels of ripe bhim kol bananas in the sun until completely brittle, then burn them to a fine white ash. Place the ash in a muslin cloth, pour water through it slowly, and collect the amber filtrate. Alternatively, use store-bought khar powder dissolved in water.
Heat mustard oil in a pot until it just smokes, then let it cool slightly.
Add the crushed garlic and slit green chilies, sauteing for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the cubed raw papaya and turmeric. Stir for a minute to coat.
Pour in the khar liquid and water. Add the soaked rice grains, which will help thicken the dish as they cook.
Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce heat and simmer uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes until the papaya is completely soft and the liquid has reduced to a thin, slightly viscous consistency.
Finish with a drizzle of raw mustard oil, adjust salt, and serve warm as the first course of an Assamese thali with steamed rice.
Trim the thick stems and central ribs from the taro leaves so they fold without cracking.
Stack 3 to 4 leaves overlapping into a cup shape in your palm, like flower petals.
Spoon 2 tablespoons of coconut cream into the center of each cup; season with a pinch of salt, a little onion, and corned beef if using.
Fold the leaf edges up and over the filling to seal each parcel; press gently to compact.
Wrap each parcel in one or two breadfruit or banana leaves and tie with kitchen twine.
Steam in a covered pot over simmering water, or in a 160C oven on a tray with a shallow layer of water.
Cook for 2 to 2.5 hours, until the taro leaves are silky-soft and the coconut cream has thickened into a custard.
Unwrap at the table and eat with the rich coconut cream that has pooled inside each parcel.
Preheat the oven to 180C. Pat the lamb dry and season with salt and pepper.
Melt half the butter in a heavy oven-safe pan (an earthenware tave is traditional); brown the lamb on all sides over high heat with the sliced garlic.
Add 250 ml of water, cover, and braise in the oven for 40 minutes.
Stir in the rice and spread it evenly through the meat; return to the oven for 10 minutes uncovered.
In a bowl, whisk together the yogurt, eggs, flour, oregano, and a pinch of salt until smooth.
Pour the yogurt custard over the lamb; dot with the remaining butter and dust the top with paprika.
Bake uncovered for 30 to 40 minutes, until the top is golden, set, and lightly puffed.
Rest for 15 minutes before serving; the custard firms as it cools.

ingredients.name: fresh sheep cheese or whole-milk ricotta

steps: Combine the flours and salt in a bowl; drizzle in the warm water and knead 8 minutes into a smooth, elastic dough. Wrap and rest 30 minutes.
Boil the potatoes whole in salted water until tender, about 25 minutes; peel while warm and pass through a ricer.
Fold the pecorino, fresh cheese, mint, garlic, and olive oil into the riced potato; season with salt and cool to room temperature.
Roll the dough to 1.5 mm thick and cut into 8 cm rounds.
Place a heaped teaspoon of filling on each round; with the seam facing up, pinch and fold the edge in alternating left-right pleats down its length, sealing into a wheat-ear shape.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a gentle simmer; cook the culurgiones 4 to 5 minutes until they float and the dough is tender.
Warm the passata with a pinch of salt and a drizzle of olive oil; lift the pasta directly into the sauce and toss gently.
Serve immediately, finished with grated pecorino and a few torn mint leaves.

ingredients.name: rugbraud or dark rye bread (to serve)

steps: Boil the potatoes whole in salted water until tender, about 20 minutes; peel while warm and chop into 2 cm chunks.
Poach the fish gently in lightly salted water with the bay leaf for 6 to 8 minutes, until just flaking. Lift out, drain, and flake into large pieces.
Melt the butter in a wide pan over medium heat; sweat the onion until translucent, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the flour and cook 1 minute, then gradually whisk in the warm milk until a smooth, loose bechamel forms.
Season with white pepper, salt, and curry powder if using.
Fold in the potatoes and the flaked fish; warm through gently without breaking the fish apart.
Serve immediately in deep bowls with thick slices of buttered rye bread.

ingredients.name: saffron threads (bloomed in 2 tbsp hot water)

steps: In a heavy pot, warm the olive oil and smen over medium heat; soften the onions and garlic 12 minutes until pale gold.
Add the ginger, ras el hanout, turmeric, bloomed saffron, fenugreek, and salt; stir for 1 minute.
Slide in the chicken and turn to coat in the spice paste; pour in 1 liter of stock and bring to a gentle simmer.
Add the lentils, partially cover, and simmer 45 minutes, topping up stock as needed; the broth should stay generous.
Tear the msemen into rough strips and warm them briefly in a dry pan.
Heap the torn msemen across a wide platter; ladle lentils and broth over until the bread softens.
Arrange the chicken on top, spoon over the caramelized onion sauce, and finish with toasted almonds and a drizzle of smen.
Eat communally, scooping bread, lentils, and chicken in every bite.

ingredients.name: chicken thighs or duck legs (skin-on, bone-in)
saffron threads (bloomed in 3 tbsp hot water)
sugar (only if molasses is very tart)

steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over low heat for 8 minutes, until fragrant but not darkened; cool, then grind to a fine paste in a food processor.
In a heavy pot, sweat the grated onion in butter over medium-low heat until deeply golden, about 12 minutes.
Brown the chicken on all sides in the same pot; remove and set aside.
Stir the ground walnuts into the onion and cook 5 minutes; pour in the water and bring to a gentle simmer.
Cover partially and simmer on the lowest possible heat for 45 to 60 minutes, stirring often, until the walnut oil rises and the sauce darkens to amber.
Stir in the pomegranate molasses, bloomed saffron, salt, pepper, and sugar if using; return the chicken to the pot.
Simmer uncovered for 30 to 40 minutes more, until the sauce reduces to a glossy near-black gravy and the chicken is meltingly tender.
Rest 10 minutes; serve over Persian saffron rice (chelow) scattered with pomegranate arils.

ingredients.name: mutton or lamb with fat (cut into 3 cm cubes)
lamb tail fat or rendered fat (curdyuk)

steps: Render the tail fat in a heavy cast-iron pan or dutch oven over medium-high heat until crackling and golden; lift out and reserve the cracklings.
In the rendered fat, sear the mutton cubes in batches until deeply browned on all sides; remove to a plate.
Lower the heat, add the onions with a pinch of salt, and let them slowly soften and brown in the meat fat for 15 to 20 minutes.
Return the meat (and offal if using) to the pan with the garlic, cumin, whole chili, and remaining salt.
Cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 1 hour, stirring once or twice; no water is added, the dish must cook in its own juices.
Uncover, raise the heat, and let the remaining liquid evaporate; the meat should glaze in the dark fat.
Stir through the dill and the reserved cracklings; serve hot, scooped onto torn non bread.
Pat the meats dry and season generously with salt and pepper.
Arrange the lamb and veal in a single layer in a wide, shallow round pan (cast iron or a traditional Croatian sac).
Tuck the onions, potatoes, garlic, rosemary, and bay leaves around and on top of the meat.
Pour the olive oil and white wine over everything and cover with a heavy domed lid (the peka itself).
Traditional method: build a wood fire, then heap glowing embers and ash up over and around the lid; roast 2.5 to 3 hours, topping up the embers as they cool.
Home oven alternative: preheat to 220C, place the covered pan on the lowest rack for 30 minutes, then lower to 170C and roast 2 hours undisturbed.
Lift the lid carefully; the lamb should pull from the bone and the potatoes should be crisp-edged and saturated in juices.
Bring the pan to the table; serve with crusty bread and a glass of Plavac Mali.

ingredients.name: firm white reef fish (walu or mahi-mahi), skinless

steps: Cut the fish into 1.5 cm cubes, checking carefully for any bones.
Place the fish in a glass or ceramic bowl and pour over the combined lime and lemon juice until fully submerged.
Cover and refrigerate for 2-3 hours, stirring once, until the fish turns opaque and firm ('cooked' by the acid).
Drain off and discard most of the citrus juice, leaving the fish just moist.
Gently fold in the coconut cream until the fish is generously coated.
Stir through the tomato, red onion, chili, and spring onion, then season with salt.
Chill for a further 30 minutes and serve cold in a halved coconut shell or glass.
Boil the potato in unsalted water until soft, then mash and reserve the cooking water; cool both to lukewarm.
Make the 'bug' (starter): mix the mashed potato, 150 g flour, sugar, and enough reserved potato water to form a thick batter in a jar.
Cover loosely and leave in a warm place for 3-5 days until bubbly, sour, and active, feeding with a little flour and water if needed.
To bake, combine the 600 g flour and salt in a large bowl and make a well in the centre.
Dissolve the baking soda in a splash of warm water and stir it through the active starter to mellow its sourness.
Add the starter and warm water to the flour and mix to a soft dough, then knead for 8-10 minutes until smooth.
Shape into a round loaf, place in a greased tin, cover, and prove for 1-2 hours until risen.
Bake at 200C for 35-40 minutes until golden and hollow-sounding when tapped; cool before slicing thickly with butter.
Build a fire and heat clean river stones in it until very hot (or use a heavy lidded cast-iron pot and oven at 160C as a home substitute).
Line a pit or roasting vessel with banana leaves, leaving plenty of overhang.
Layer the sweet potato and taro on the bottom, then the pork chunks, seasoning each layer with salt.
Add the bananas and pile the aibika greens over the top.
Pour the coconut cream evenly over everything so it can steam through the food.
Fold the banana leaves over to seal the parcel tightly and, in a traditional mumu, cover with hot stones and earth.
Leave to steam undisturbed for about 2.5-3 hours until the pork is tender and the kaukau is soft.
Unwrap at the table and serve the meat, root vegetables, and greens together from the leaves.

ingredients.name: cow foot, cleaned and cut into pieces

steps: Boil the cow foot with chopped onion, stock cubes, and salt until very tender and gelatinous, about 1.5-2 hours; reserve a little stock.
Dissolve the potash in a few tablespoons of water and let the sediment settle, then pour off the clear liquid.
In a clean pot, gently warm the palm oil (do not bleach it) and stir in the potash liquid; it will thicken and turn the oil pale and creamy.
Stir in the ground ehu seeds, ground crayfish, dried chili, and a little reserved stock to form a thick yellow sauce.
Fold the warm cow foot pieces through the sauce until every piece is glossy and well coated.
Season to taste and warm through gently.
Serve in a wooden mortar (okwa) topped with sliced raw onion and shredded utazi leaves, with chilled stout or palm wine.

ingredients.name: fresh whole cow or goat milk
charcoal embers from senetwet (African olive) or guava wood

steps: Scald the milk by bringing it to a gentle boil, then let it cool to room temperature.
Char a small piece of clean hardwood until glowing, then use it to scrub and smoke the inside of the dry gourd or jar until coated with fine ash.
Pour the cooled milk into the smoke-lined gourd and seal it.
Leave to ferment at room temperature for 3-5 days, swirling once a day, until thick, tangy, and faintly grey from the charcoal.
Taste from day 3 onward and refrigerate once the desired sourness and smoky flavour develop.
Shake well and serve cold in a cup or gourd alongside ugali or roast meat.

ingredients.name: fermented corn dough (for the sour batter)

steps: Whisk a few tablespoons of maize flour and the fermented corn dough into 500 ml cold water to make a thin slurry.
Bring the slurry to a simmer, stirring constantly, until it thickens into a light, slightly sour porridge.
Gradually beat in the remaining maize and millet flour a little at a time, stirring vigorously over low heat until you have a smooth, stretchy, stiff dough.
Add splashes of hot water as needed and keep turning the dough for 8-10 minutes until glossy and lump-free, then shape into wet balls.
For the ayoyo soup, boil the jute leaves with chopped tomato, onion, dawadawa, ground pepper, and salt until soft and slippery.
Blend or mash the soup lightly to release its characteristic mucilaginous texture and simmer to combine.
Serve the warm TZ balls in a bowl with the ayoyo soup poured alongside, eaten by pinching the dough and dipping.
Make the bara dough: combine flour, turmeric, cumin, yeast, sugar, and salt, then add warm water to form a soft, sticky dough.
Cover and let rise in a warm place for 1.5-2 hours until doubled.
Meanwhile, boil the soaked channa until very soft, then drain, reserving a little liquid.
Bloom the curry powder with garlic in hot oil, add the channa, cumin, salt, and a splash of water, and simmer until thick and some chickpeas break down.
Heat frying oil to 180C. Wet your hands, pull off small balls of dough, and flatten into thin discs.
Fry each bara for about 20-30 seconds per side until puffed and just cooked but still soft; drain.
For each serving, overlap two bara, spoon curried channa in the centre, and top with tamarind chutney and pepper sauce to taste.
Fold and eat immediately while soft.

ingredients.name: goat head and tripe, cleaned and chopped

steps: Wash the goat head, feet, and tripe thoroughly with lime or vinegar, then place in a large pot and cover generously with water.
Bring to a boil, skim off the foam, then add garlic, scallion, thyme, and salt and simmer for about 2 hours until the meat is tender and the broth is gelatinous.
Add the green bananas, yam, and cho-cho and cook until soft, about 25 minutes.
Make spinners by mixing flour with a little water and salt into a stiff dough, then roll pea-sized pieces between your palms into thin dumplings and drop into the pot.
Add the whole scotch bonnet (do not burst it unless you want intense heat) and simmer 10 minutes more.
Stir in the white rum at the very end and adjust salt.
Serve piping hot in bowls as a celebratory starter.
Simmer the turkey pieces in salted water with half the onion until the meat is tender and a rich broth forms, about 1.5 hours; reserve the broth.
Toast the dried guaque and cobanero chilies briefly in a dry pan, then soak in hot water until soft.
Char the tomatoes, tomatillos, garlic, and remaining onion on a comal or under a broiler until blistered.
Blend the soaked chilies, charred vegetables, achiote, and a ladle of the turkey broth into a smooth red paste.
Strain the paste back into the broth and bring to a simmer, stirring, until the soup turns clear and deep red.
Return the turkey to the pot, add the mint, cilantro, and samat, and simmer 15-20 minutes to infuse the herbs.
Adjust salt and serve hot with small white corn tamalitos and white rice.
Soak the chuño in water for several hours, then squeeze out the moisture and break or grate into small pieces.
In a large pot, brown the lamb and beef, then add the onion, garlic, cumin, and yellow aji paste and fry into a fragrant sofrito.
Cover with plenty of water and bring to a boil, then add the pre-soaked mote and wheat berries and simmer for about 45 minutes.
Add the chuño and fresh potatoes and continue cooking until everything is tender, about 30 minutes more.
Stir in the fava beans and peas and simmer until soft.
Season with salt and oregano, mashing a few potatoes against the side of the pot to thicken the broth.
Serve hot in deep bowls, ideally with a spoonful of fresh llajwa chili sauce on the side.
